item.title: Flecha Dev Log #34: Returning References and Slices
item.description:
Introduction

Hi folks!

Flecha had checked references. It had checked slices. We could borrow a variable, pass the borrow into a function, prevent conflicting access while it was live, and release the restriction after its last use.

It felt like we had everything.

Then we tried to return a slice.

The slice itself is only an address and a length. Returning those bits is easy. The real question is whether the storage behind them remains alive, and which value in the caller must remain borrowed while the returned view is used.

Then the same problem appeared when returning a reference to a structure field.

How do we make sure the borrowed lifetime stays in scope? How do we carry that relationship through a call while preserving Flecha’s existing last-use and exclusivity rules?

That is what this dev log is about.

The missing relationship

Consider a function that returns the tail of a slice:

[]const i32 tail([]const i32 values) {
    return values[1:];
}

The return type tells us that the result is a read-only slice. It does not say where the slice came from.

If it came from values, the caller’s original sequence must stay borrowed. If it came from a local array, returning it must be rejected because that array disappears with the call. If a function receives two slices, the result type alone cannot tell us which argument anchors the returned view.

References have exactly the same gap:

&const i32 value(&const Box self) {
    return &self->value;
}

The compiler can see the origin inside this body, but callers need that relationship in the function’s contract. Once the function is registered in another module or instantiated through a generic, its implementation cannot be the caller’s lifetime model.

Name the source

Flecha now writes that relationship with <- source:

[]const i32 tail([]const i32 values) <- values {
    return values[1:];
}

&const i32 value(&const Box self) <- self {
    return &self->value;
}

Read it as “the returned borrow comes from this parameter.”

The contract is compile-time information. It does not add a lifetime object, reference counter, hidden allocation, or extra field to a slice. References and slices keep their native representation.

The named source must be a checked reference or checked slice parameter. A raw pointer, owning pointer, ordinary value, local variable, or temporary cannot anchor a safe returned loan. Even an unsafe block cannot manufacture that proof.

Every result containing a checked reference or checked slice requires a contract. A contract on a function that returns no borrowed value is also an error. The syntax describes one exact relationship; it is not a decorative annotation.

The callee proves the origin

Every reachable return path is checked against the declared source.

Returning the source itself is valid. So is returning a checked reborrow derived from it: a structure field, a fixed-array element, a fixed-array slice, a slice element, or a subslice. Returning a reference to a local or to another parameter is rejected even if the types look identical.

Permission can become weaker, never stronger:

&T       -> &T          allowed
&T       -> &const T    allowed
&const T -> &const T    allowed
&const T -> &T          rejected

[]T       -> []T          allowed
[]T       -> []const T    allowed
[]const T -> []const T    allowed
[]const T -> []T          rejected

A function may expose less access than it received. It cannot turn shared access into exclusive mutation.

The caller inherits the loan

At a call site, the compiler substitutes the actual argument’s origin into the returned value:

values := [10, 20, 30, 40];
rest := tail(values[:]);

stdoutln(rest[0]);
values[1] = 21;

While rest is live, it protects the original sequence according to ordinary borrow rules. Its last use is rest[0], so the later mutation is valid.

Move that mutation before the stdoutln and the compiler rejects it: the read-only slice still borrows the sequence. Try to move, rebind, or destroy the source while the result is live and the same protection applies.

The returned handle participates in everything Flecha already knows: exclusivity, last-use analysis, parent reborrows, field projections, moved handles, branches, loops, and scope exits. We did not need a second borrow checker. We needed the call boundary to preserve the information the existing checker was missing.

Contracts compose

A contracted function may return the result of another contracted function when the inner loan ultimately comes from the outer function’s declared source:

[]const i32 skip_two([]const i32 values) <- values {
    return tail(tail(values));
}

The origin survives nested calls, module boundaries, generic specialization, and recursion. The compiler stores the source parameter in the function symbol, then substitutes the caller’s concrete origin each time the function is used.

This is where the architectural choice pays off. The relationship is part of the function’s semantic contract, so it does not disappear after parsing or depend on inlining the body.

More than one result

A single source can produce a flat tuple containing borrowed results:

structure Pair {
    i32 left;
    i32 right;
};

(&i32, &i32) fields(&Pair pair) <- pair {
    return (&pair->left, &pair->right);
}

Pair pair = none;
left, right := fields(&pair);
*left = 20;
*right = 22;

Each destination receives its own origin, projection, mutability, movement, and last-use state. Distinct structure fields can be proven disjoint, so the two mutable results above are valid.

Returning the same mutable place twice is rejected. Mixing a mutable result with an overlapping shared result is rejected too. Mutable array and slice elements remain conservative whole-sequence loans, so two mutable element results are rejected even when their runtime indices happen to differ.

The compiler accepts disjointness it can prove, not disjointness we merely expect.

Why immediate destructuring matters

A tuple containing borrowed values must be consumed through immediate destructuring:

left, right := fields(&pair);

Storing that borrowed tuple, nesting it, passing it as an ordinary aggregate, or capturing it in defer is rejected.

Immediate destructuring gives every returned handle an independent tracked state at the exact call site. Supporting a stored aggregate of loans would require the aggregate itself to preserve and expose several lifetime relationships. Until that model exists, keeping the operation flat makes the accepted behavior honest.

What the contract does not do

<- does not turn raw pointers into checked references. It does not let a safe API borrow arbitrary heap storage whose owner relationship is unknown. It does not cover returned stringv, external C references, or several independent source parameters.

These boundaries are intentional. A single source is precise enough to state, validate, compose, and explain, so the accepted feature stays within what the caller can prove today.

Conclusion

Returning a reference or slice was never mainly about returning an address. It was about returning a relationship.

<- source makes that relationship part of the function contract. The callee proves that every borrowed result comes from the declared parameter; the caller keeps the corresponding storage borrowed for exactly as long as the result remains live.

No garbage collector, hidden allocation, or runtime lifetime table is required. We preserve the origin, enforce the permission, and let last-use analysis do the rest.

This is the kind of Flecha problem I love: the syntax is tiny, but it carries exactly the information needed to make a low-level operation feel direct and still remain checked.

I hope you liked this write-up and learned something new. As always, don’t forget to do your research!

item.title: Flecha Dev Log #33: A Complete Development Environment
item.description:
Introduction

Hi folks!

A compiler rarely lives alone. A real session also needs the standard library, project tool, linker, editor support, and a place where all those pieces agree about paths and versions.

When that agreement depends on the original repository or one developer’s shell configuration, we do not have an environment. We have a collection of local coincidences.

Flecha now discovers its installed pieces as one toolchain and can reproduce the entire setup inside a disposable development sandbox.

The installed standard library

Longbow projects can import the bundled standard library without manually mapping its source directory:

module main;

@imports
    :: lib::std::io::filesystem;

i32 main() {
    contents, err := filesystem::read_file("message.txt");
    if err != none {
        return 1;
    }

    stdoutln(contents);
    return 0;
}

The installed Longbow executable locates its version-matched lib::std relative to the toolchain layout. Moving a complete installation keeps the relationship intact because discovery does not point back to the checkout that produced it.

Explicit project libraries still use configured names. Automatic discovery is reserved for the standard library shipped with the same toolchain, where a predictable default removes setup without hiding dependency resolution.

Destructuring that fits real APIs

As standard APIs returned more tuples, bindings needed to handle the common case where one result is new and another already exists:

quotient, err := divide(20, 3);
next, err := divide(42, 5);

i32 first, second = (20, 22);
first, i32 third = (second, 42);

With :=, at least one non-blank name must be new in the current scope. New names are declared and existing names in that scope are assigned. With =, an explicit type introduces a declaration while an untyped name refers to an existing destination.

The entire right-hand side evaluates once before any store occurs. That preserves swaps, lets old values participate in the expression, and prevents one destination from changing what a later destination receives.

This looks like a syntax improvement, but it plugs directly into definite assignment, cleanup, and borrow checking. Each new or existing binding must leave those analyses with one unambiguous state.

The sandbox

The Docker development sandbox builds the current checkout and installs the result into a clean Linux environment:

make sandbox
make enter-sandbox

Inside it, flecha and longbow are on PATH, the installed standard library is discovered automatically, Clang 18 is available for native linking, and a starter project waits in /workspace/hello:

cd /workspace/hello
longbow check
longbow run
nvim src/main.fl

The shell runs as an unprivileged flecha user. The repository is mounted read-only, so the environment can inspect current sources without quietly changing the host checkout.

Editor configuration without host pollution

When a host Neovim configuration exists, the sandbox copies it into the disposable container. Plugin managers may update lockfiles, caches, and downloaded plugins there without touching the host.

If no configuration exists, a minimal one enables Flecha file detection and syntax highlighting. The installed Neovim plugin and the current compiler therefore meet in the same isolated session.

Rebuilding the sandbox replaces the container. Anything important must be copied out, which is a useful reminder that the environment is reproducible by design, not precious state to maintain forever.

One command tests many contracts

make sandbox exercises more than Docker packaging. It checks that installation paths are relocatable, Longbow finds the standard library, native linking prerequisites are sufficient, editor files are installable, permissions are reasonable, and a fresh user can build a real project.

That is the value of bringing the pieces together: the environment tests the boundaries between components, where otherwise-correct tools most often disagree.

Conclusion

Flecha’s development environment now has a coherent shape. The toolchain finds its own standard library, tuple results fit natural binding patterns, and one disposable sandbox brings compiler, Longbow, linker, editor support, and a starter project together.

The result is a wonderfully practical milestone: enter the environment and write Flecha. The setup itself no longer needs to be the experiment.

I hope you liked this write-up and learned something new. As always, don’t forget to do your research!

item.title: Flecha Dev Log #32: Stabilizing the First Toolchain
item.description:
Introduction

Hi folks!

There is a point in a young language where adding another feature is easier than reconciling everything already built.

We chose reconciliation.

Flecha 0.1.1 is a stabilization release: compiler crashes and misleading diagnostics were fixed, packages were tested as installations, toolchains were pinned, editor artifacts were added, and the documentation was brought back into agreement with the implementation.

Stability is a feature

A compiler should reject an invalid program with a useful source range. It should not crash because an unexpected type survived too far into lowering. It should not emit an object after a mandatory ownership check failed. It should not vary its answer because one code path forgot the rule another code path enforces.

The stabilization pass concentrated on those seams: parser recovery, semantic diagnostics, native-driver failures, installed-path discovery, portability, and release packaging.

This work is less visible than new syntax, but it changes how confidently we can use every existing feature.

Documentation is tested behavior

Early project documents naturally contain plans mixed with implementation. Over time, that becomes dangerous. A reader cannot tell whether a paragraph describes code they can run or an idea we still like.

The 0.1.1 documentation distinguishes shipped behavior from proposals. Compiler commands, LLVM support, linking requirements, checked references, slices, allocation analysis, ownership contracts, generics, ABI limits, and cross-platform constraints are described according to the toolchain that exists.

The test suite and documentation now share the same boundaries. When a limitation is real, we say it. When a workflow is promised, a clean installation exercises it.

One release, one revision

The release condition is deliberately holistic. The full protected matrix must pass from one revision: ordinary tests, sanitizer coverage, packaging, clean installation, editor validation, native output, and platform checks.

That prevents a familiar failure mode where the Linux fix exists on one commit, the Windows package fix on another, and the published tag corresponds cleanly to neither.

The compiler, Longbow, runtime, standard library, VSIX, Neovim files, documentation, archives, and checksums are treated as one versioned toolchain.

The boundary is public

A release archive bundles the LLVM runtime it needs. Native executable builds still rely on a documented host linker and SDK. The standard library is found through the installed layout. Editor packages have verifiable versions. Unsupported compiler and LLVM combinations fail during configuration.

These decisions define which problems belong to Flecha and which prerequisites belong to the host. Stability improves when that boundary is explicit enough to test.

What stabilization feels like

The satisfying outcome is not a spectacular demo. It is repetition without surprise:

flecha check src/main.fl
longbow build
longbow run

The same project survives a clean machine, a relocated archive, and each supported platform. A failure names the missing piece. The docs describe the command we actually shipped.

That is a different kind of progress from growing the syntax. It is the progress of making a tool dependable enough that attention can return to the program being written.

Conclusion

Flecha 0.1.1 gave the first installable toolchain a firmer floor. It aligned diagnostics, packages, supported versions, editor artifacts, and documentation around one tested release.

Building a language is not only inventing semantics. It is also making those semantics arrive intact on another machine.

I hope you liked this write-up and learned something new. As always, don’t forget to do your research!

item.title: Flecha Dev Log #31: Shipping the Editor Experience
item.description:
Introduction

Hi folks!

Syntax highlighting often begins as a small grammar checked into the repository. That is enough for its author, who knows where it lives and how to wire it into an editor.

It is not enough for somebody who downloaded a compiler archive and wants .fl files to look like Flecha files.

We turned editor support into versioned, tested release artifacts for Visual Studio Code and Neovim.

A real VSIX

Visual Studio Code support is packaged as flecha-language-VERSION.vsix. It can be checksum-verified and installed directly:

sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing
code --install-extension flecha-language-VERSION.vsix

The extension supplies file detection, syntax highlighting, comments, brackets, and indentation. Its stable identity is flecha.flecha-language, so installing a newer VSIX upgrades the same extension instead of creating a sibling.

The packaging command uses a locked Node dependency graph and a pinned official VSIX builder. It validates the extension identity and version, checks the installation manifest and grammar, and ensures development-only files do not leak into the archive.

The release workflow also checks that the extension version matches the release tag. A Flecha archive and its editor package should tell the same version story.

Neovim as a native package

Neovim support ships inside the compiler archive at share/flecha/editors/neovim. Copying it into a normal pack/*/start directory makes it load as a native package:

mkdir -p ~/.local/share/nvim/site/pack/flecha/start
cp -R /path/to/flecha/share/flecha/editors/neovim \
  ~/.local/share/nvim/site/pack/flecha/start/flecha.nvim

Open a .fl file and :set filetype? should report flecha. Filetype detection, syntax groups, buffer settings, and indentation are exercised headlessly in tests.

For a development checkout, a symbolic link points Neovim directly at the grammar. For a release, copying the packaged directory keeps the installation tied to that toolchain version.

Highlighting must follow the language

New syntax is not finished when only the compiler recognizes it.

Generic parameters, enum declarations, match arms, ownership annotations, imports, and borrowed-result contracts all need editor grammar updates. Otherwise valid code looks broken precisely when users are trying to learn the feature.

Treating editor tests as part of the main suite catches drift between parser syntax and the tools people stare at all day.

Clear limits

These packages provide syntax and editing basics; they are not a language server. There is no claim of semantic completion, rename, project-wide references, or inline diagnostics.

That distinction matters. A small reliable editor integration is more useful than a package whose description promises intelligence it does not contain.

Conclusion

Editor support became part of the distribution rather than a repository curiosity. Visual Studio Code gets a verified VSIX; Neovim gets a tested runtime package; both travel with install, upgrade, verification, and removal instructions.

A language starts feeling real long before self-hosting. Sometimes it happens the first time a source file opens with the right name, indentation, and colors without a private setup ritual.

I hope you liked this write-up and learned something new. As always, don’t forget to do your research!

item.title: Flecha Dev Log #30: Defining a Supported Toolchain
item.description:
Introduction

Hi folks!

“Requires LLVM” sounds like documentation until the compiler builds with one version, CI uses another, and a release silently picks up whatever a rolling package manager installed that morning.

Support needs a definition that the build system can enforce.

Flecha now has one toolchain policy connecting local configuration, continuous integration, release production, and clean-install verification.

Ranges for source builds

Source builds accept explicit version ranges:

  • CMake 3.20 or newer;
  • LLVM development packages from 17 through 23;
  • Clang from 17 through 23;
  • GCC from 13 through 16;
  • Apple Clang from 16 through 17;
  • a C and C++ compiler from the same toolchain with C++23 support.

CMake detects these versions before compilation and rejects unsupported or incomplete combinations. When LLVM is installed outside the default search path, LLVM_DIR points at its CMake package directory.

Failing at configuration is much kinder than reaching hundreds of compiler errors caused by an incompatible LLVM API.

Pinned release baselines

Ranges are appropriate for contributors. Release artifacts need tighter baselines.

Linux x86-64 is produced on Ubuntu 24.04 with Clang and LLVM 18. Windows x86-64 uses the MSYS2 UCRT64 environment with Clang and LLVM 23. macOS x86-64 and arm64 use macOS 15, Homebrew Clang and LLVM 18 for the build, and Xcode 16.4 with Apple Clang 17 for native linking.

Each release job prints and verifies the compiler, LLVM, linker, target, platform runtime, and SDK versions. A package-manager update cannot quietly change the compiler that produced the release.

Builders and users need different things

Building Flecha from source requires LLVM development files. Running a Flecha release archive does not: the archive carries its matching LLVM shared runtime.

Users who build native executables still need the host’s linker driver and system development or SDK components. That distinction is now explicit in both documentation and clean-install tests.

It avoids two opposite mistakes: telling users to install an entire compiler-development stack they do not need, or suggesting native linking can work without the platform pieces only the operating system can provide.

Policy lives in code

The supported ranges are not prose copied into a README and forgotten. CMake policy, CI matrices, release workflows, and documentation change together.

Adding a compiler or LLVM major means exercising the full suite: regular tests, sanitizers, packaging, installed layouts, clean consumers, and platform-specific native output. “It configured on my machine” is useful evidence, but it is not the support bar.

Why this is architectural

Flecha’s backend uses LLVM, its driver invokes platform-native tools, and its release packages must be relocatable. The version matrix is where those three systems agree.

Writing it down forced hidden assumptions into the open: which LLVM APIs we rely on, which C++ language level the compiler uses, which Windows runtime we target, and which macOS SDK produced a compatible archive.

Conclusion

A supported toolchain is a tested contract, not an optimistic list of software names.

Flecha now rejects unsupported combinations early, pins the environments that create releases, verifies what actually ran, and separates source-builder requirements from archive-user requirements.

It is not the flashiest compiler feature, but it is one of the things that makes every other feature reproducible.

I hope you liked this write-up and learned something new. As always, don’t forget to do your research!

item.title: Flecha Dev Log #29: Making Linker Failures Actionable
item.description:
Introduction

Hi folks!

Native compilation has an awkward seam. Flecha can successfully parse, check, and lower a program, emit a correct object file, and then depend on a host C++ driver to produce the executable.

When that last step fails, “linker exited with code 1” is technically true and practically useless.

We changed linker discovery and reporting so the compiler explains what it attempted and what the machine is missing.

Build has distinct stages

The command line exposes the compiler’s stopping points:

flecha check input.fl
flecha --emit-llvm input.fl
flecha --emit-object input.fl -o input.o
flecha build input.fl -o input

Only the last command needs the native linker. This matters for diagnostics: a user checking source should not be told to install an SDK that the requested operation never uses.

It also gives us a clean fault boundary. If object emission succeeds and executable linking fails, the error belongs to host toolchain discovery or invocation rather than Flecha’s frontend.

Discovery you can explain

On each platform, Flecha searches a documented set of suitable C++ drivers. It records which candidates were attempted instead of discarding that information.

If none can be used, the diagnostic lists the attempted driver names and gives platform-specific prerequisites: development and startup files on Linux, the UCRT64 Clang environment on Windows, or Xcode command-line tools and a macOS SDK on macOS.

When a driver launches but linking fails, Flecha includes the actual linker output. We should never hide the one message that names an undefined symbol, missing library, or incompatible architecture.

An authoritative override

Automatic discovery is convenient until a machine has several toolchains. FLECHA_LINKER selects a driver name or full path:

FLECHA_LINKER=/opt/llvm/bin/clang++ flecha build src/main.fl -o app

The override is authoritative. If it is invalid, Flecha reports that failure instead of silently falling back to another compiler and producing a binary with a toolchain the user did not select.

That behavior is especially useful in CI and reproducible build environments, where an unexpected fallback is often worse than a clear failure.

Temporary output must be safe

Executable builds first emit Flecha code to a unique temporary object and then invoke the native driver.

Using a unique path avoids an easy but destructive collision: if the requested executable is named program and the user links a nearby program.o, compiler output must never overwrite that input object. Temporary artifacts are implementation details; user-supplied link inputs are not disposable.

The same rule makes concurrent builds and repeated invocations much less surprising.

Runtime discovery is part of the story

An installed compiler finds its version-matched runtime library relative to its own executable. A development override exists for diagnostics, but installed layouts do not depend on the repository that produced them.

When linking fails because that runtime is absent or unusable, the error identifies the expected location. The diagnostic should connect the user’s action to the missing component, not ask them to understand compiler internals first.

Conclusion

Error reporting is part of toolchain design. Flecha now distinguishes frontend work from native linking, explains driver discovery, respects an explicit override, preserves linker output, and offers advice for the actual platform.

The goal is simple: a failed build should leave us with the next action, not a mystery.

I hope you liked this write-up and learned something new. As always, don’t forget to do your research!

item.title: Flecha Dev Log #28: Testing the Installation, Not the Checkout
item.description:
Introduction

Hi folks!

A compiler passing tests inside its own repository proves less than it first appears. The checkout contains source files, build metadata, generated artifacts, and paths that an installed user will never have.

A release can be green in CI and still fail the moment somebody unpacks it elsewhere.

Flecha’s release tests now treat the archive as a downstream user would: install it cleanly, move it, and build programs using only what the distribution promises.

The archive is the product

The important artifact is not the build directory. It is the archive containing flecha, Longbow, the runtime library, the standard library, editor support, licenses, and documentation in their installed layout.

The smoke test unpacks that archive into a clean location and deliberately relocates it before running anything. If a binary accidentally remembers an absolute build path, relocation exposes the mistake immediately.

The installed compiler must find its matching runtime relative to itself. Longbow must find the bundled standard library without a source-tree hint. A project must compile and link without reaching back into the original checkout.

Consume it like a user

The clean environment asks the same questions a new installation will:

flecha --version
longbow --version
longbow check
longbow build
longbow run

It also compiles direct single-file programs, exercises native output, checks local project dependencies, and verifies the packaged files themselves.

This is an inversion worth emphasizing. Instead of testing internal targets and assuming packaging preserves them, the test begins with the package and sees whether public workflows survive.

Host tools are explicit

The archive carries the LLVM runtime it needs, so users do not need LLVM development headers merely to run Flecha. Producing a native executable still needs a host linker driver and platform startup files or SDK.

Clean-install jobs provide only those documented prerequisites. If the archive works only because a full development environment happened to be preinstalled, the test should fail.

Object emission and frontend checking remain useful distinctions: flecha check and --emit-object do not invoke the system linker, while an executable build does.

Every platform is a consumer

Linux, Windows under MSYS2 UCRT64, macOS x86-64, and macOS arm64 each run the archive as a fresh consumer.

That is not one generic packaging test repeated four times. Paths, dynamic libraries, executable suffixes, native drivers, SDK discovery, archive formats, and shell behavior differ. The common contract is that an installation contains everything Flecha owns and clearly reports anything the host must supply.

Release engineering is language work

Modules, the runtime ABI, the standard library, native linking, and Longbow all meet inside the installed directory tree. A broken relative path can make a correct language feature unusable.

Testing the public installation therefore protects architecture, not just packaging. It forces compiler and tooling components to agree on what the distribution boundary actually is.

Conclusion

The strongest release test starts by forgetting how the repository was built.

By consuming a relocated archive in a clean environment, Flecha verifies the experience we are actually offering: unpack the toolchain, create or open a project, and build native code with documented host prerequisites.

That makes a release feel less like a compressed build directory and more like a product we can hand to someone else.

I hope you liked this write-up and learned something new. As always, don’t forget to do your research!

item.title: Flecha Dev Log #27: Exhaustive Enum Matching
item.description:
Introduction

Hi folks!

An enum defines a closed set of possibilities. Once the compiler knows that set, asking programmers to reconstruct exhaustiveness with a chain of if statements would waste the most useful information the type provides.

Flecha’s match is an expression that evaluates one enum value once, selects one arm, and requires the cases to be complete.

Match produces a value

Because match is an expression, it fits directly into a return or assignment:

i32 precedence(TokenKind kind) {
    return match kind {
        TokenKind.Identifier => 1,
        TokenKind.Number => 2,
        TokenKind.End => 0,
    };
}

Every arm contains an expression. The enclosing declaration, argument, assignment, or return can provide its expected type; otherwise the first arm establishes the result type and the remaining arms must be assignable to it.

Only the selected arm executes. The input expression itself executes exactly once, so a call or increment used as the subject cannot be duplicated by lowering.

Exhaustiveness is checked

Without a wildcard, every variant must appear exactly once. Missing a variant is a compile-time error. So are duplicate variants, unknown variants, and variants from another enum.

This turns enum growth into useful pressure. Add a new token kind, rebuild, and every complete match that needs a decision points directly at the missing behavior.

For cases where several values intentionally share behavior, _ covers everything not already named:

bool TokenKind::ends_input(&const self) {
    return match *self {
        TokenKind.End => true,
        _ => false,
    };
}

The wildcard must be the last arm. Code after it would be unreachable, and Flecha reports that instead of silently accepting a misleading list.

A focused pattern language

The initial pattern language has two forms: a qualified enum variant and _.

There are no guards, ranges, integer or string patterns, destructuring patterns, or block-bodied arms here. Keeping the first version narrow made it possible to define exhaustiveness, typing, evaluation order, and code generation without pretending to support a general pattern system.

That focus also keeps match aligned with its purpose: making decisions over a closed nominal type.

Lowering to a switch

The compiler lowers the expression to a switch over the enum’s backing integer. Every valid representation reaches one arm.

When the source lists every variant and has no wildcard, impossible integer representations become unreachable in the backend. When _ exists, it becomes the default edge. The source-level completeness proof therefore maps neatly onto efficient native control flow.

Conclusion

match lets the enum declaration do real work. It removes repeated comparisons, keeps value production concise, and makes forgotten cases a compiler problem.

The part I enjoy most is how direct the code reads: here is one value, here are all of its meanings, and here is the result for each one.

I hope you liked this write-up and learned something new. As always, don’t forget to do your research!

item.title: Flecha Dev Log #26: Enums Are Real Types
item.description:
Introduction

Hi folks!

Named integer constants are useful until the compiler forgets what they mean. A token kind and a connection state may both fit in a byte, but that does not make them interchangeable.

Flecha enums are nominal, allocation-free scalar types. They retain the efficiency of an integer representation while giving the type checker a closed vocabulary of values.

Declaration and representation

An enum may choose its backing integer and discriminants:

export enum TokenKind: u16 {
    default NoToken = 0,
    Identifier,
    Number = 10,
    End,
}

The backing type defaults to u32. Implicit discriminants begin at zero and continue from the preceding value; explicit values can create meaningful gaps. Signed backing types permit negative values.

The compiler checks that each value fits its backing type and that both names and discriminants are unique. The enum lowers to its integer representation, but that representation does not erase the declared type.

TokenKind.Identifier and a variant from another enum remain incompatible even when both happen to equal one. There are no automatic integer-to-enum or enum-to-integer conversions.

Qualified values

The enum name is a type, not a value. Variants stay qualified:

TokenKind kind = TokenKind.Identifier;

if kind == TokenKind.End {
    stdoutln("done");
}

Qualification makes the domain visible at each use and avoids filling module scope with generic names such as End, Open, or None.

Equality and strict equality work between values of the same enum. Arithmetic, ordering, increment, implicit truth tests, and cross-enum comparison do not. An enum describes alternatives; it is not an integer wearing a label.

A semantic default

At most one variant can be marked default. That variant gives contextual none a useful meaning:

enum State: u8 {
    Off,
    default Unknown = 7,
    On,
}

State state = none;       // State.Unknown
[3]State states = none;   // every element is State.Unknown

The default is semantic, so it does not need discriminant zero. Arrays and structures initialize the actual selected value rather than clearing bytes and assuming the result is meaningful.

Without a default variant, contextual none is rejected. A variable can still be declared for later assignment, and definite-assignment analysis prevents premature reads.

Behavior without boxing

Enums can have out-of-line methods using the same receiver model as structures:

bool State::is_on(&const self) {
    return *self == State.On;
}

void State::turn_on(&self) {
    *self = State.On;
}

Read-only, mutable, pointer, static, private, and generic methods follow the language’s existing rules. No object header or heap allocation is introduced; the value is still the backing scalar at runtime.

Enums may be stored in structures, tuples, fixed arrays, generic containers, references, and raw pointers. Their initialization and destruction remain compiler-defined because scalar enums have no custom lifecycle hooks.

Conclusion

Enums close a gap between representation and meaning. The machine gets a compact integer; the programmer gets a distinct type, qualified values, checked defaults, and methods.

It is a small feature on the surface, but it gives many APIs a much sharper vocabulary.

I hope you liked this write-up and learned something new. As always, don’t forget to do your research!

item.title: Flecha Dev Log #25: Crossing the C Boundary
item.description:
Introduction

Hi folks!

A native language eventually needs to call code it did not compile. Operating systems, mature libraries, and even a language’s own runtime often meet at the C ABI.

The tempting implementation is “let the linker figure it out.” Flecha took the opposite approach: make the boundary narrow, explicit, and strict enough that unsupported representations fail before linking.

An extern is only a declaration

An external function has a Flecha signature but no Flecha body:

extern unsafe i32 native_read(
    *const char path,
    usize path_length,
    *u8 output,
    usize capacity
);

The native linker supplies the implementation. The exported symbol is exactly native_read, without a Flecha module prefix, while name lookup inside Flecha still respects the module that declared it.

External declarations must be free, non-generic functions. They cannot be lifecycle overrides or the program entry point. These restrictions keep language-specific calling behavior away from a boundary that promises the C ABI.

Extern and unsafe mean different things

extern says where the implementation comes from. unsafe says what responsibility the call carries.

A scalar-only external function can be safe:

extern i32 native_add(i32 left, i32 right);

A signature containing raw pointers must be unsafe, and every call needs ordinary unsafe permission. A raw pointer crossing this boundary gains no ownership, lifetime, aliasing, provenance, or nullability guarantee simply because its declaration has a type.

Flecha also refuses to pass tracked owning or lent allocations to an external function. Until an external ownership contract can describe what native code does with that memory, the safe answer is not to guess.

A deliberately small ABI

The first ABI supports void, integer and floating-point scalars, bool, char, and raw pointers. Narrow integer arguments receive the sign or zero extension required by the target C ABI.

References, slices, tuples, structures, error values, and strings by value are rejected. Their in-memory forms are Flecha implementation details, not accidental C interfaces.

Strings expose bytes explicitly with data() inside unsafe code, while length travels separately. Two versioned runtime handles support the compiler’s own string bridge, but ordinary libraries see byte pointers and lengths.

Linking is part of the command

Executable builds accept repeatable native inputs:

flecha build src/main.fl -o app --link native_io.o --link libmath.a

Longbow records the same objects or archives in the project manifest. Object emission deliberately stops before the linker, keeping “compile this module” distinct from “assemble this executable.”

Filesystem I/O as a real test

The standard library uses this boundary to offer safe whole-file reading:

@imports
    :: lib::std::io::filesystem;

contents, err := filesystem::read_file("input.fl");
if err != none {
    return err;
}

The wrapper validates the path, calls a versioned runtime function, and receives one owned string on success. Empty files succeed with an empty string. Embedded null bytes and platform line endings are preserved because contents are bytes, not secretly decoded text.

Errors distinguish missing files, denied permission, invalid paths, oversized contents, failed reads, and allocation failure. The file is closed and partial storage is released on every path.

On POSIX, paths travel as byte sequences. On Windows, UTF-8 paths are validated and converted to UTF-16 before opening. Those differences belong in the runtime wrapper, not in every Flecha program.

Conclusion

Interoperability is safest when neither side is asked to pretend. Flecha names the C-compatible subset, makes raw memory calls visibly unsafe, preserves ownership checks at the edge, and wraps platform details in a safe standard API.

The boundary is intentionally small. Small boundaries are easier to understand, test, and trust.

I hope you liked this write-up and learned something new. As always, don’t forget to do your research!
